title: The AHA Just Said Exercise Works Even When the Scale Does Not Move. South Asians Need to Hear This.
excerpt: A new scientific statement in Circulation documents that physical activity improves blood pressure, insulin resistance and visceral fat independently of weight loss
body:
The American Heart Association has published a new scientific statement in its journal Circulation that might change how you think about the relationship between exercise and your bathroom scale. The core message: physical activity delivers profound cardiovascular and metabolic benefits even when your weight barely changes.

The Statement That Upends Common Thinking

The scientific statement, authored by Damon L. Swift and colleagues, synthesises the current evidence on the role of physical activity in obesity treatment and cardiometabolic health. The most important finding for desk-bound professionals may be this: exercise alone typically produces only modest weight loss and is unlikely to result in the clinically meaningful threshold of a 5 per cent reduction in body weight.

But that does not mean it is failing.

The statement documents that regular physical activity improves blood pressure, insulin resistance, and lipid profiles independently of weight loss. It reduces visceral fat — the dangerous abdominal fat surrounding internal organs — even when the number on the scale stays put. It preserves lean muscle mass during calorie restriction and improves cardiorespiratory fitness, which is itself a powerful predictor of longevity.

Why South Asians Need to Hear This

South Asians carry a disproportionate burden of metabolic disease. Indian Americans are two to four times more likely to develop type 2 diabetes than their white counterparts, often at lower body weights. The conventional South Asian body type — thin limbs with central adiposity — means BMI alone is a particularly unreliable guide to metabolic health.

This is precisely the population for whom the AHA's message matters most. If you are a 40-year-old NRI professional who started running or hitting the gym six months ago and your weight has barely moved, the science now says you are almost certainly healthier anyway. Your blood vessels are more flexible, your cells are responding better to insulin, and the visceral fat wrapping your liver and pancreas is likely shrinking even if your subcutaneous fat looks the same in the mirror.

The GLP-1 Equation

The statement also addresses the interaction between physical activity and the new wave of anti-obesity medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide. While these drugs produce dramatic weight loss, the AHA warns that up to 40 per cent of the weight lost on GLP-1 drugs can come from lean muscle mass rather than fat. Physical activity, particularly resistance training, can shift that ratio towards greater fat loss and muscle preservation.

For the growing number of South Asians on these medications — a population already prone to lower muscle mass relative to fat — this distinction is critical. The drugs without exercise may improve the scale number while quietly eroding the muscle that protects metabolic health.

What the Evidence Says You Should Actually Do

The statement reinforces existing guidelines: aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity per week, plus two sessions of resistance training. But it adds nuance. For weight-loss maintenance — keeping lost weight off — the evidence suggests you may need more, on the order of 200 to 300 minutes per week of moderate activity.

The good news is that even falling short of these targets delivers benefits. The dose-response curve is steepest at the low end: moving from nothing to something produces the largest improvement in cardiovascular risk factors. A 30-minute daily walk is not a consolation prize for failing to become a marathon runner. It is a clinically meaningful intervention.

The Accessibility Problem

The AHA statement also calls for multidisciplinary collaboration to make exercise accessible and affordable, particularly for underresourced populations with higher rates of obesity. This resonates across the diaspora. First-generation NRIs often work long hours, have family obligations that crowd out gym time, and may live in areas without safe walking infrastructure.

Community-based solutions — walking groups at temples and gurudwaras, workplace wellness challenges, family weekend hikes — may be more culturally sustainable than individual gym memberships. The science says consistency matters more than intensity: a daily evening walk after dinner does more long-term good than sporadic weekend warrior sessions.

Sources: Swift LD et al., "Role of Physical Activity in Obesity Treatment and Cardiometabolic Health: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association," Circulation (2026), DOI: 10.1161/CIR.0000000000001441; American Heart Association EPI Lifestyle Scientific Sessions 2026
